issues.issue: The Custodian must list any document that 'does not meet the requirements of Section 2.01' as an exception, yet is simultaneously barred from determining whether endorsements are sufficient, whether assignments are in recordable form, or whether certain documents belong in the file. The review duty and the carve-outs from it cover much the same ground.

The repurchase obligation arises only if the defect 'materially and adversely affects the interests of the Certificateholders or the Certificate Insurer in the related Mortgage Loan,' with no standard for materiality and no allocation of the burden of showing it. Whether a given document defect triggers repurchase is left at large.

The cure-or-repurchase obligation is declared 'the sole remedies respecting such defect available to the Trustee, the Master Servicer, the Depositor and any Certificateholder,' an enumeration that omits the Certificate Insurer and the NIMS Insurer, to whom the Agreement elsewhere gives enforcement and reimbursement rights. Whether the insurer is confined to the same sole remedy turns on that omission.

For representations made 'to the best of the Transferor's knowledge,' the provision deems an inaccuracy a breach 'notwithstanding the Transferor's lack of knowledge,' so the qualifier is given and taken away in the same sentence. What a knowledge-qualified warranty means here is the question the clause creates.

The deemed-material list runs to 'clauses (xiii), (xiv), (xv) and (xxxv) through (l) of Schedule II,' where '(l)' can be read as the roman numeral fifty or as the letter l, and the trigger elsewhere in the same paragraph shifts between the interests of the Certificateholders 'or' and 'and' the Certificate Insurer. Which representations are automatically material, and whose interests must be affected, is unclear.

This paragraph gives the Transferor ninety days from discovery or notice to cure a representation breach, while Section 2.02 imposes a separate ninety-day cure-or-repurchase regime for document defects on the same loans. Which regime governs a defect that is both is not addressed.

Here the Substitution Adjustment Amount is computed by the Master Servicer as the shortfall between substitute and deleted loan balances and is remitted by the Transferor, whereas the Section 1.01 definition frames it as arising on a Mortgage Loan 'purchased by the ... originator.' The two statements of the same defined term do not match.

The sole-remedy sentence lists 'Certificateholders, the Master Servicer, the NIMS Insurer, the Depositor, the Trust Administrator or the Trustee' but not the Certificate Insurer, whose enforcement and reimbursement rights appear in the same Section 2.03. Whether the Certificate Insurer is bound by the sole-remedy limitation is left to inference from the list.

Discovery of a breach of the Section 2.04 representations requires only prompt written notice; no cure, repurchase or substitution obligation or any other remedy is attached, unlike the Section 2.03 regime. What follows a breach of the Depositor's title warranty is unstated.

The Trustee agrees here to perform its duties 'to the best of its ability, to the end that the interests of the Holders ... may be adequately and effectively protected,' while Article VIII limits the Trustee to the duties expressly set out and negates implied covenants. The standard of the Trustee's obligation cannot be taken from this section alone.

The representation is satisfied if 'the Master Servicer or an affiliate thereof' is an approved Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac servicer and HUD-approved mortgagee, so it warrants nothing about the Master Servicer itself. What is warranted about the contracting party is left indeterminate.

The Master Servicer must act 'with customary and usual standards of practice of prudent mortgage loan master servicers' while also having 'full power and authority to do any and all things which it may deem necessary or desirable.' Neither the prudent-master-servicer standard nor the limits on that discretion is defined.

Tax and insurance costs are not to 'be added to the Scheduled Principal Balances of the related Mortgage Loans,' using a term the Agreement does not define; the defined balances are 'Principal Balance' and 'Stated Principal Balance.' The quantity that may not be increased is unnamed.

Whether a Servicer is to be terminated rests on the Master Servicer's own 'judgment,' after which it may 'issue such notice or take such other action as it deems appropriate,' with no standard or obligation fixed. The provision creates a duty measured only by the obligor's discretion.

The Master Servicer 'shall' terminate a non-performing Servicer, yet the same paragraph makes enforcement a matter of what it 'in its good faith business judgment, would require were it the owner of the related Mortgage Loans.' The mandatory and discretionary formulations of the same duty conflict within the provision.

The Master Servicer may reimburse itself from the Collection Account for termination and transfer costs 'including, without limitation' two broadly described categories, with no cap and no requirement of reasonableness. The scope of the charge against trust collections is open-ended.

The Master Servicer must evaluate a consent request 'in the best interest of the Trust and the Certificateholders' and act 'promptly or within the time frame specified in such Servicing Agreement, if any,' leaving both the standard and the deadline indefinite where the Servicing Agreement is silent. The Certificate Insurer's interest is not mentioned at all.

This section says neither the Trustee nor the Depositor has any responsibility for the Master Servicer's acts or any duty to supervise it, while Section 3.05 and Section 7.02 require the Trustee to assume the Master Servicer's obligations on a Master Servicer Event of Termination. How far the Trustee's disclaimer survives its succession duties has to be worked out between them.

The carve-outs refer to losses of the predecessor Master Servicer 'pursuant to Section 3.09 hereof' and to expenses 'pursuant to Section 2.03,' but Section 3.09 concerns access to documentation and does not deal with losses. The scope of the successor's exemption rests on miscited sections.

The Master Servicer must 'use its best efforts to effect the orderly and efficient transfer' of the subservicing agreements, a standard the Agreement neither defines nor measures. What effort discharges the duty is left open.

If the Master Servicer does not pay within thirty days the cost becomes 'an expense of the Trust' payable out of the Distribution Account, 'provided that the Master Servicer shall reimburse the Trust for any such expense' — the same obligation it has just failed to perform. The proviso leaves the Trust with a circular remedy.

Item (iii) requires deposit of 'all Recoveries,' a capitalized term the Agreement does not define (it defines 'Subsequent Recoveries'), and items (x) and (xi) refer to 'the Mortgage Loans in such Loan Group' although no Loan Group has been identified in the sentence. What must be deposited is uncertain in those respects.

Realized investment losses in the Collection Account are to be deposited by the Master Servicer 'in the Collection Account or paid to the Trust Administrator ... for deposit into the Distribution Account,' without saying who chooses between the two. The destination of the make-whole payment is left unfixed.

This subsection repeats verbatim the Eligible Account covenant already made in Section 2.01(e), including the sub-account proviso. Two identical covenants in different articles invite argument over whether they were meant to operate differently.

The Carryover Reserve Fund is held 'in trust for the benefit of the Holders of the Offered Certificates,' while the following paragraph directs its investment for the benefit of the Class C Certificateholders and provides that the Class C Certificates evidence ownership of the fund. The identity of the beneficial owner is stated two ways.

The exculpation is for investments 'made in accordance with this Section 3.05,' although the Carryover Reserve Fund and its investments are governed by Section 3.07(h) in which the sentence appears. The exculpation is tied to the wrong section.

Cap Account investments are made 'for the benefit of the Supplemental Interest Trust, on behalf of the Holders of the Offered Certificates,' yet the same paragraph provides that 'the Class C Certificates shall evidence ownership of the Cap Account' and gives the Class C Holders the investment direction. Who owns the account and its earnings is stated inconsistently.
